routes.speaker: Tyler Vela
routes.position: The observed absence or ambiguity of divine presence conflicts with Christianity's claim that God is perfectly loving and seeks redemptive relationship.

bridges.statement: Essentially perfect Christian love and a divine aim of redemptive relationship create an expectation of sufficient personal availability that observed hiddenness conflicts with.
Biblical fatherhood and commands to imitate divine love require recognizable continuity with loving parental presence rather than an analogy in which absence becomes love.
Sincere seekers and former believers can remain without adequate awareness of God and suffer apostasy or salvation risk despite their willingness to relate.
God could have created unfallen agents or conditions that support freedom, virtue, and robust belief without first producing the broken circumstances invoked to justify hiddenness.
Hiddenness defenses that appeal to fallen suffering merely relocate the challenge unless the necessity and proportionality of that suffering are established.
Modest, periodic, or broadly corroborated revelation could reduce nonbelief and improve redemptive relationship without forcing love or requiring exhaustive disclosure.

routes.speaker: Michael Jones
routes.position: Christian divine hiddenness is compatible with perfect love because calibrated disclosure can serve sanctification, right-motive relationship, freedom, soul formation, and just judgment.

bridges.statement: Perfect love can permit calibrated hiddenness when overt presence would foster use, rebellion, or distorted relationship rather than freely sanctified love.
God seeks cognitively robust, morally transformative theism for right motives, not mere assent produced by abundant evidence.
God judges agents according to their knowledge and excuses genuine nonresistance, with postmortem opportunity remaining plausible, so hiddenness need not cause unjust loss.
Real struggle enables triumphant good and historically formed virtue that could not be authentically replicated by simply installing finished character.
God's eternal perspective and humanity's fallen agency materially qualify comparisons between divine governance and an ordinary human father's conduct.
Given Christianity's fallen-world premises, hiddenness can be internally coherent even when broader questions about why suffering exists require a separate theodicy.
Because motives are complex and individual, an omniscient God may tailor the timing and degree of disclosure rather than follow a universal evidential rule.
